speakers: Tobias J. Moskowitz (University of Chicago Booth, NBER; consultant to AQR)
Lasse Heje Pedersen (NYU Stern, Copenhagen Business School, AQR, CEPR, FRIC, NBER)
summary: Do value and momentum premia exist, and co-move, across eight markets/asset classes (4 stock markets, country index futures, currencies, government bonds, commodities), and what drives them? Using uniform simple signals (BE/ME or negative 5-year return; 12-1 month return), tercile and rank-weighted long-short factors (1972-2011), correlations, PCA, macro/liquidity regressions and asset-pricing tests, they find positive premia everywhere, strong cross-asset comovement, negative value-momentum correlation, partial funding-liquidity exposure, and propose a global three-factor model (MKT, VAL, MOM everywhere).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We find consistent value and momentum return premia across eight diverse markets and asset classes, and a strong common factor structure among their returns.
claims.claim: Value and momentum earn positive return premia in all eight markets/asset classes studied, and their returns share a strong common factor structure.
claims.indicator: value and momentum long-short factors in 8 asset classes
claims.direction: long cheap / long winners, short expensive / short losers

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Value and momentum returns correlate more strongly across asset classes than passive exposures to the asset classes, but value and momentum are negatively correlated with each other, both within and across asset classes.
claims.claim: Value strategies co-move with value in other asset classes (and momentum with momentum) more than the passive asset classes co-move, while value and momentum are negatively correlated with each other.
claims.indicator: cross-asset correlations of value and momentum factors

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Global funding liquidity risk is a partial source of these patterns, which are identifiable only when examining value and momentum jointly across markets.
claims.claim: Exposure to global funding liquidity risk partly explains value/momentum comovement, and this is only detectable when pooling many markets.
claims.indicator: funding liquidity risk (TED spread, LIBOR-term repo, swap-T-bill)
claims.testable: yes - regress factor returns on funding liquidity shocks

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Our findings present a challenge to existing behavioral, institutional, and rational asset pricing theories that largely focus on U.S. equities.
claims.claim: Because the premia and their correlations appear in non-equity asset classes, theories built for U.S. stocks alone cannot fully explain them.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: AQR Capital invests in, among other things, value and momentum strategies.
claims.claim: Authors disclose a commercial interest: their employer/consultancy invests in value and momentum strategies.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: (individual stocks in the United States, the United Kingdom, conti- nental Europe, and Japan; country equity index futures; government bonds; currencies; and commodity futures)
claims.claim: The study universe is eight asset classes: stock selection in US, UK, continental Europe and Japan, plus country equity index futures, government bonds, currencies and commodity futures.
claims.exact_rule: apply identical value and momentum construction separately inside each of 8 asset classes

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: including value and momentum in government bonds and value effects in currencies and commodities, which are all novel to the literature.
claims.claim: Value and momentum in government bonds and value in currencies and commodities are new findings of this paper.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Our broader set of portfolios generates much larger cross-sectional dispersion in average returns than those from U.S. stocks only
claims.claim: The 48 cross-asset test portfolios spread average returns much more widely than U.S.-stock portfolios, giving a tougher test for pricing models.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Value strategies are positively correlated with other value strategies across otherwise unrelated markets, and momentum strategies are positively correlated with other mo- mentum strategies globally.
claims.claim: Value in one market positively co-moves with value in unrelated markets; likewise for momentum - the central comovement finding.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: using a simple three-factor model consisting of a global market index, a zero-cost value strategy applied across all asset classes, and a zero-cost momentum strategy across all assets
claims.claim: The proposed pricing model has three factors: a global market index, a global all-asset value factor and a global all-asset momentum factor.
claims.exact_rule: factors: MKT (MSCI World), VAL everywhere, MOM everywhere (zero-cost, signal-weighted, inverse-vol aggregated across asset classes)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: stocks with high positive momentum (high 6- to 12-month past returns) outperform stocks with low momentum (Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), Asness (1994))
claims.claim: Prior work: U.S. stocks with high past 6-12 month returns outperform low-momentum stocks; value stocks outperform growth stocks (Stattman, Rosenberg et al., Fama-French 1992).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Momentum is also found in currencies (Shleifer and Summers (1990), Kho (1996), LeBaron (1999)) and commodities (Erb and Harvey (2006), Gorton, Hayashi, and Rouwenhorst (2008)).
claims.claim: Prior literature already documented momentum in currencies and commodities and value/momentum in country equity indices.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: three-factor model does a good job capturing the returns to the Fama and French U.S. stock portfolios as well as a set of hedge fund indices.
claims.claim: The global three-factor model prices the Fama-French U.S. stock portfolios and hedge fund indices well.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We show that separate factors for value and momentum best explain the data, rather than a single factor, since both strategies produce positive returns on average yet are negatively correlated.
claims.claim: Two separate factors are needed because both value and momentum earn positive means while being negatively correlated, which one factor cannot reproduce.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A single factor would require significant time variation in betas and/or risk premia
claims.claim: A single-factor explanation would need strongly time-varying betas or premia; the authors stay agnostic whether their two factors are separate unconditional factors or capture such dynamics.
claims.testable: partly - conditional single-factor model not tested

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We find only modest links to macroeconomic variables such as the business cycle, con- sumption, and default risk.
claims.claim: Macro variables (business cycle, consumption, default risk) explain little of value and momentum returns.
claims.indicator: GDP, recession, consumption growth, default spread

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: liquidity risk is negatively related to value and positively related to momentum globally across asset classes.
claims.claim: Across asset classes momentum loads positively and value negatively on liquidity risk.
claims.direction: value suffers / momentum benefits in liquidity improvements (and vice versa)

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Sadka (2006) find that measures of liquidity risk are positively related to momentum in U.S.
claims.claim: Earlier work linked U.S. stock momentum to liquidity risk; this paper extends the link to other markets and to value (negative).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: implying that part of the negative correlation between value and momentum is driven by opposite signed exposure to liquidity risk.
claims.claim: Opposite-signed liquidity exposures partly account for the negative value-momentum correlation.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: the primary link between value and momentum returns comes from funding risk, whose importance has increased over time, particularly af- ter the funding crisis of 1998.
claims.claim: Funding liquidity (not market liquidity) is the main liquidity link, and it has strengthened over time, especially after 1998.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The statistical power gained by looking across many markets at once—a unique feature of our analysis—allows these factor exposures to be revealed.
claims.claim: Pooling many markets gives the statistical power needed to detect liquidity exposures that single-market studies miss.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: liquidity risk can only explain a small fraction of value and momentum return premia and comovement.
claims.claim: Economically, liquidity risk explains only a small part of value/momentum premia and comovement.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: because value loads negatively on liquidity risk, the positive premium associated with value becomes an even deeper puzzle.
claims.claim: Since value is a liquidity hedge yet earns a positive premium, liquidity risk deepens rather than resolves the value puzzle.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: is immune to liquidity risk and generates substantial abnormal returns.
claims.claim: An equal-weight value+momentum combination has no net liquidity exposure but still earns large alpha, so funding risk cannot explain the combination premium.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: such correlation structure is not a prediction of existing behavioral models
claims.claim: Cross-asset comovement could reflect common global risk factors and is not predicted by existing behavioral models (Daniel-Hirshleifer-Subrahmanyam, Barberis-Shleifer-Vishny, Hong-Stein).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: In addition to assuaging data mining concerns, evidence of consistent value and momentum premia across diverse asset classes
claims.claim: Finding the same premia in many unrelated asset classes reduces data-mining concerns (out-of-sample in asset space).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: These theories seem ill equipped to explain the same and correlated effects we find in currencies, government bonds, and commodities.
claims.claim: Rational theories based on firm investment or growth options (Gomes-Kogan-Zhang, Zhang, Berk-Green-Naik, etc.) cannot explain value/momentum in currencies, bonds, commodities.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: a simple combination of the two is much closer to the efficient frontier than either strategy alone, and exhibits less variation across markets and over time.
claims.claim: Because value and momentum are negatively correlated with positive means, a combination is much more efficient and more stable than either alone.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Fama and French (2012) examine the returns to size, value, and momentum in in- dividual stocks across global equity markets and find consistent risk premia across markets.
claims.claim: Related global evidence: Fama-French (2012) global stock premia; Frazzini-Pedersen betting against beta; Koijen et al. carry; Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen time-series momentum.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Time- series momentum is a timing strategy using each asset’s own past returns, which is separate from the cross-sectional momentum strategies we study here.
claims.claim: The paper studies cross-sectional (relative) momentum, distinct from time-series momentum which times each asset on its own past return.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: The link to funding liquidity risk may also be consistent with global arbitrage activity in the face of funding constraints influencing value and momentum returns (Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009)).
claims.claim: Funding-constrained global arbitrage capital (Brunnermeier-Pedersen) may drive the liquidity link in value and momentum returns.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: momentum represents the most popular trades, as investors chase returns and flock to the assets whose prices appreciated most recently.
claims.claim: Momentum positions are crowded because investors chase recent winners.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Value, on the other hand, represents a contrarian view.
claims.claim: Value positions are contrarian, hence less crowded.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: investors engaged in liquidating sell-offs (due to cash needs and risk management) will put more price pressure on the most popular and crowded trades, such as high momentum securities
claims.claim: In a liquidity shock forced sellers hit crowded momentum trades hardest (everyone runs for the exit, Pedersen 2009), so momentum loses when liquidity dries up.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: while the less crowded contrarian/value trades will be less affected.
claims.claim: Less crowded value trades suffer less in liquidating sell-offs, giving value a negative liquidity-risk loading relative to momentum.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: They argue that flows between investment funds can give rise to momentum effects from inertia due to slow moving capital, and eventually push prices away from fundamentals causing reversals or value effects.
claims.claim: Vayanos-Woolley: fund flows under delegated management create momentum via slow-moving capital and later reversal (value) when prices overshoot fundamentals.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Correlation of value and momentum across different asset classes could also be affected by funds flowing simultaneously across asset classes, which could in turn be impacted by funding liquidity.
claims.claim: Simultaneous fund flows across asset classes, driven by funding liquidity, could produce the cross-asset correlation of value and momentum.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: However, matching the magnitude of our empirical findings remains an open question.
claims.claim: Whether these flow/delegation models can match the empirical magnitudes is unresolved.

claims.quote: our goal is to maintain a simple and fairly uniform approach that is consistent across asset classes and minimizes the pernicious effects of data snooping.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we use the common value signal of the ratio of the book value of equity to market value of equity, or book-to-market ratio, BE/ME

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Book values are lagged 6 months to ensure data availability to investors at the time, and the most recent market values are used to compute the ratios.
claims.claim: Book equity is lagged 6 months for availability, divided by the most recent (current) market value.
claims.exact_rule: value_i,t = BE_(t-6m) / ME_t

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: When using more recent prices in the value measure, the negative correlation between value and momentum is more negative and the value premium is slightly reduced, but our conclusions are not materially affected.
claims.claim: Using more recent prices in BE/ME makes value-momentum correlation more negative and slightly lowers the value premium, without changing conclusions.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: A combination of value and momentum—one of the themes in this paper—obtains nearly identical pricing results regardless of whether we lag price in the value measure.
claims.claim: The value+momentum combination's pricing results are insensitive to whether price is lagged in the value measure.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Asness and Frazzini (2012) investigate this issue more thoroughly and argue that using contemporaneous market values can be important
claims.claim: Asness-Frazzini (2012) argue contemporaneous market values matter when studying value alongside momentum.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Gerakos and Linnainmaa (2012) decompose value into book and market components and find that the market value of equity drives most of the relevant pricing information.
claims.claim: Gerakos-Linnainmaa: the market-value component drives most of BE/ME's pricing information, supporting price-based value proxies.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: we use the common measure of the past 12-month cumula- tive raw return on the asset
claims.claim: Momentum signal is the past 12-month cumulative raw return skipping the most recent month (MOM2-12).
claims.exact_rule: mom_i,t = prod(1+r_i,t-12..t-2) - 1

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: We skip the most recent month, which is standard in the momentum literature, to avoid the 1-month reversal in stock returns, which may be related to liquidity or microstructure issues
claims.claim: The latest month is skipped to avoid 1-month reversal from liquidity/microstructure effects.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: While research has shown that other value measures are more powerful for predicting stock returns
claims.claim: Better stock value measures exist (Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny, Asness-Porter-Stevens, Piotroski) but BE/ME is kept for simplicity and consistency.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Novy-Marx (2012) shows that the past 7- to 12-month return is a better momentum predictor in U.S. stocks than the past 2- to 6-month return
claims.claim: Novy-Marx: in U.S. stocks months 7-12 predict better than months 2-6 (though 2-6 still positive).

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Momentum is straightforward since we can use the same measure for all asset classes, namely, the return over the past 12 months skipping the most recent month.
claims.claim: The same MOM2-12 signal is used in every asset class.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: Momentum returns for these asset classes are in fact stronger when we don’t skip the most recent month, hence our results are conservative.
claims.claim: For index futures and currencies (less liquidity-affected) momentum is stronger without the skip month; skip kept for uniformity.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For country indices, we use the previous month’s BE/ME ratio for the MSCI index of the country.

claims.exact_rule: value_c,t = BE/ME of MSCI country index at t-1

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: For commodities, we define value as the log of the spot price 5 years ago (actually, the average spot price from 4.5 to 5.5 years ago), divided by the most recent spot price

claims.exact_rule: value = ln(mean(spot over months t-66..t-54) / spot_t)
claims.direction: long commodities that fell most over 5 years

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: for currencies, our value measure is the negative of the 5-year return on the exchange rate, measured as the log of the average spot exchange rate from 4.5 to 5.5 years ago
claims.claim: Currency value = log(avg spot 4.5-5.5 years ago / spot today) minus the log foreign-vs-US CPI change over the same period: the 5-year change in purchasing power parity.
claims.exact_rule: value = ln(mean S_(t-66..t-54)/S_t) - [ln(CPI_f,t/CPI_f,t-60) - ln(CPI_us,t/CPI_us,t-60)]

claims.quote: For bonds, we use the 5-year change in the yields of 10-year bonds as our value measure, which is similar to the negative of the past 5-year return.

claims.speaker: authors
claims.quote: These long-term past return measures of value are motivated by DeBondt and Thaler (1985), who use similar measures for individual stocks

reasoning.question: Are value and momentum premia a U.S.-stock curiosity or a pervasive feature of all liquid markets, do they share common sources across asset classes, and what single parsimonious model could describe global multi-asset returns? For an investor this decides whether value and momentum can be diversified across asset classes, whether a value+momentum combination is a robust core allocation, and what risks (e.g., funding liquidity) the positions carry.

thesis.statement: Value and momentum earn positive premia in every major asset class, value co-moves with value and momentum with momentum across unrelated markets while the two are negatively correlated, and a global market+value+momentum model prices these portfolios, U.S. stock portfolios and hedge funds better than U.S. factors; funding liquidity risk explains part of the comovement (especially after 1998) but not the premia, and the 50/50 combination remains a large, liquidity-neutral puzzle.

foundations.premise: A premium that appears with the same simple signal in many unrelated asset classes is unlikely to be a data-mining artifact; uniform simple measures are an out-of-sample test.
foundations.support: intuition; deliberate choice of standard signals; asserted that better signals would raise returns

foundations.premise: Long-horizon past price declines (negative 5-year return, 5-year PPP change, 5-year yield rise) measure 'cheapness' in assets that have no book value, just like BE/ME in stocks.
foundations.support: DeBondt-Thaler, Fama-French 1996, Gerakos-Linnainmaa; own test: 0.83 (U.S.) and 0.86 (global) correlation between 5-year-return and BE/ME value factors

foundations.premise: Past 12-month return skipping the latest month captures momentum in every asset class; the skip month avoids a short-term reversal tied to liquidity/microstructure.
foundations.support: standard in literature (Jegadeesh-Titman, Asness, Goyal-Wahal), out-of-sample record

foundations.premise: Comovement of long-short, market-neutral strategies across markets with different investors and institutions points to a common global risk factor rather than market-specific behaviour.
foundations.support: interpretation of correlation and PCA evidence; argued that behavioral models do not predict it

foundations.premise: Equity-specific rational theories (firm investment, growth options) and individual-investor behavioral theories cannot generate correlated effects in currencies, bonds and commodities.
foundations.support: argument, citations to the theories; no formal test

foundations.premise: Momentum trades are crowded (return chasing) while value trades are contrarian, so forced liquidations in funding shocks hit momentum harder.
foundations.support: intuitive story (Pedersen 2009 'run for the exit'); crowding is not measured

foundations.premise: Liquidity risk carries a positive risk premium.
foundations.support: Fama-MacBeth liquidity-beta premium of 24 bp/month (t=3.05) among the 48 portfolios; earlier literature

foundations.premise: Averaging strategies across many markets diversifies idiosyncratic noise so a weak common exposure becomes detectable.
foundations.support: Figure 4: average individual t-stats -0.95/1.81 vs -3.25/4.43 for the averaged series

foundations.premise: Large, liquid universes (top 90% of market cap; futures) give implementable and conservative estimates because premia are larger in small illiquid securities.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Cross-sectional ranks of (a) multi-year cheapness - negative 5-year price/real exchange-rate change, 5-year rise in 10y yields or (better) real yield and term spread for bonds, BE/ME for stocks and country indices - and (b) 12-1 month relative returns are the inputs that lead returns over the next month (rebalanced monthly; effect horizon roughly months to a few years). They work through slow-moving capital/return chasing (momentum) and later overshoot correction (value), with risk compensation and funding constraints in the background. Funding liquidity shocks (TED, LIBOR-repo, swap-T-bill spreads; AR(2) residuals) are contemporaneous drivers, not predictors: worsening funding hurts momentum and helps value. What would make them stop working: arbitrage capital crowding raising correlations (seen post-1998), sharp liquidity rebounds that crash momentum (2009), and for value long bubbles (1999-2000); the 50/50 mix is the version least exposed to these regime swings.
reader_inferences: (reader) The combo factor column in Table I appears rescaled (not a literal 0.5/0.5 average) for several asset classes; scaling not stated.

(reader) Table VII post-1998 conditional Sharpe ratios look arithmetically inconsistent with the unconditional post-1998 row, and Table VII Sharpe levels match the P3-P1 tercile spreads rather than the rank factors.
(reader) Large value drawdowns around 1999-2000 and a momentum drop around 2009 are visible in Figure 2 but not discussed in the text.
(reader) Bond value (baseline measure) does not share the common factor (PC1 loading ~0) and has a deep 1980s-early 1990s drawdown, so bond results are fragile.
(reader) Funding-liquidity regressions use contemporaneous shocks; they describe risk exposure, not a timing signal.
(reader) Ex post volatility weights and full-sample normalisation mean the published Sharpe ratios are not exactly implementable; costs would lower stock strategies most.

(reader) Part of the three-factor model's pricing success on the 48 portfolios is mechanical because VAL/MOM factors are built from the same securities (equation 5), which the authors acknowledge; the leave-one-out equation (4) R2 of 0.55 is the cleaner evidence.
